justification: Re-read the whole article, the round-1 adsense review (9.0), and diffed the current draft against the exact commit round 1 scored (58e6ea9) to isolate what actually changed before judging it. Two new comparators this round, chosen to be unlike round 1's listicle/table pages: bigocheatsheet.com's sorting section is a pure complexity-notation reference table (13 algorithms, best/average/worst/space columns) with no code, no stability discussion, no lower-bound proof and no language-specific built-in-sort behavior; toptal.com's sorting-algorithms page is an animation/visualization tool across four initial conditions with a stated 'there is no best sorting algorithm' takeaway but, by its own scope statement, no runnable code, no measured benchmarks, no stability analysis and no comparison-sort lower bound. Neither competes with what this article does: implement and count five algorithms with real machine output, prove and then numerically bracket the Omega(n log n) floor against an exhaustive 40,320-permutation scan, empirically demonstrate stability across all five plus Array.Sort/OrderBy on one ticket dataset, and tie all of it to dotnet/runtime source for introsort's actual thresholds. Re-ran `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/algorithms/sorting-algorithms-compared.md` myself from PowerShell: PASS blocks=28 executed=14, matching the writer's claim exactly. Checked each of the five stated round-2 changes directly against a diff of the reviewed round-1 commit: (1) The final 'Measure it' exercise now leads with the exact C(n) = 2(n+1)H_n - 4n formula and reports 2.6%/7.1%/6.0% instead of the old 20-30% claim. I independently recomputed C(n) for n=100/1,000/10,000 by hand (H_100 approx 5.187 -> 647.7; H_1000 approx 7.485 -> 10985.0; H_10000 approx 9.7876 -> 155774), matching the article's 647.9/10985.9/155771.7 to within harmonic-sum rounding, so the math is genuine, not asserted. The new prose explicitly cross-references the quicksort-cost block's plain-quicksort shuffled result (10,134 comparisons at n=1,000) as 'barely below' Array.Sort's own 10,202, and notes both sit inside the 10,134-10,556 range the four-seed exercise already established -- this is a real, checkable admission that the article's own earlier measurement nearly matches Array.Sort, not a hedge or a contradiction. It reads as honest self-correction exactly per the brief's never-inflate rule: it names the old headline, says why it was loose (comparing to the crude leading-order term instead of the exact average), and leaves the reader with a smaller, better-supported number instead of quietly deleting the old one. (2) The toolchain statement (.NET 10, SDK 10.0.401, runtime 10.0.12, Windows 11, Core i7-11700K, Random change in .NET 6) is placed immediately before the quicksort-cost code block -- the first block whose output depends on a seeded Random -- not in the opening paragraph, which avoids the exact 'manufactured provenance' pattern round 1 flagged in tcp-vs-udp. I independently verified this is not decorative: `dotnet --version` on this machine returns 10.0.401 and `dotnet --list-runtimes` shows 10.0.12 runtimes installed; `(Get-CimInstance Win32_Processor).Name` returns '11th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-11700K @ 3.60GHz', matching the article's CPU claim exactly. The Random-algorithm-changed-in-.NET-6 claim is accurate (the runtime replaced the legacy LCG-based algorithm with a new implementation in .NET 6, which is why a fixed seed does not reproduce pre-.NET-6 output). (3) The permutation-count output is un-wildcarded (min=12, max=17, average=15.7) and run-code confirms these are the real executed values, not typed-in guesses; the following prose uses all three numbers ('the gap is one comparison: 17 is only one above the proven floor of 16') rather than restating them decoratively, so this reads as genuinely informative, not padding. (4) The two quotation-casing fixes are correct, not cosmetic. I fetched the live dotnet/runtime source: the IntrosortSizeThreshold comment in Array.cs begins 'Empirically, 16 seems to speed up...' (capital E) and the pivot comment in ArraySortHelper.cs begins 'Compute median-of-three. But also partition them, since we've done the comparison.' (capital C) -- both sentence-initial in the source. The article quotes them mid-sentence ('a comment that "[e]mpirically..."' and 'a comment reading "[c]ompute..."'), so the bracketed lowercase letter is the standard, correct convention for altering a quoted letter's case to fit surrounding grammar. The round-1 draft had actually misquoted these as unbracketed lowercase ('empirically', 'compute'), which technically understated the source's own capitalization; round 2's fix is a genuine accuracy improvement, correctly attributed, not prose dressed as an original quote. (5) The table split (5-column 'Choosing a sort' table into a 2-column Algorithm/Worst-case table plus a bulleted Stable/Best-for list, and the exercise-1 trace table from 5 columns to 3) preserves every data point from the pre-split version -- I checked all seven rows' stable/best-for text and all four trace-table rows against the round-1 commit and found no content dropped, only reformatted; the table split also adds a short explanatory sentence pointing to where extra-space was already covered per algorithm, which is a small net gain in clarity, not filler. No ad code, no consent/analytics changes, no new unsupported claims, no keyword stuffing, and the ten front-matter sources are unchanged and were already confirmed real and correctly quoted in round 1 -- I re-spot-checked the two now-bracketed source quotes above and they still match. One soft attribution is worth a note (see issues) but does not amount to fabrication. Score is nudged up from round 1's 9.0 because this round fixes a real category of issue (a sibling article's provenance-placement finding, a genuine misquote, an inflated headline number, wildcarded output) with verifiably correct, well-placed fixes and introduces nothing new to hold it down; it stays short of a clean 10 only for the one attribution nit below and because, as in round 1, a full first-page live search ranking survey for 'sorting algorithms' could not be completed (WebSearch budget was exhausted this session after two comparator fetches), so 'confirmed best live result' rather than 'clearly ahead of the results checked' is still not fully established.

issues.location: Final 'Measure it' exercise solution, parenthetical: '(CLRS derives this refinement in its quicksort chapter)'
issues.problem: The C(n) = 2(n+1)H_n - 4n closed form is real, standard, and numerically verified correct (I recomputed it independently), but this is an inline attribution to a page-inaccessible textbook rather than one of the ten cited, URL-linked sources, and I could not confirm from any fetchable source that CLRS's chapter 7 presents this exact closed form (as opposed to deriving the O(n log n) bound via indicator random variables and stopping short of the harmonic closed form, which is how the 3rd edition's main text does it). Nothing here reads as fabricated -- the formula and numbers are correct regardless of who first wrote it down -- but the specific attribution is a claim the article cannot back up with a link the way its other 15+ inline citations do.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either soften to something ownership-neutral ('a standard refinement of the leading-order term, via the same indicator-random-variable argument CLRS uses to derive the O(n log n) bound') or, if the writer has page-level confirmation CLRS 4th ed. states this exact closed form, add a chapter/section pointer the way the other CLRS citation on this page (the comparison-sort lower bound, chapter 8) already does.
